questions.question: What is the job of a cost-based query optimizer?
options: Rewrite the user's SQL into more efficient SQL before execution
Enumerate candidate join orders and access paths, estimate each plan's IO cost from statistics, and execute the cheapest one
Cache the results of previous queries so repeats are free
Choose which indexes to build based on the query workload
questions.explanation: The optimizer turns declarative SQL into a physical plan by costing alternatives — join order, join algorithm, scan vs index — with table statistics, then runs only the winner; a 100× speedup over the naive ordering is normal. It picks among existing access paths; building indexes is a separate design decision.

questions.question: Trying all join orders for an n-table query is n! plans — infeasible. How do optimizers make the search tractable?
options: They always join tables in the order they appear in the FROM clause
They sample a few hundred random orders and keep the best
Dynamic programming: compute the cheapest sub-plan for each subset of tables once and reuse it, collapsing n! work to about 2ⁿ
They delegate ordering to the storage engine at runtime
questions.explanation: The key insight is that the best plan for a subset of tables doesn't depend on how the rest will be joined, so each subset is solved once and memoized — 2ⁿ subsets instead of n! orderings. FROM-clause order is exactly the naive behavior optimizers exist to avoid.

questions.question: A production query suddenly takes hours. pg_class.reltuples claims Listens has 1,000 rows, but it actually has a billion. What happened, and what is the standard fix?
options: Statistics are stale, so the optimizer picked a plan tuned for tiny data; run ANALYZE to refresh them
The table hit PostgreSQL's row limit; the fix is partitioning
The index on Listens is corrupted; the fix is REINDEX
The buffer pool is undersized; the fix is more RAM
questions.explanation: Cost estimates are only as good as the statistics behind them: believing Listens is tiny, the optimizer chooses small-data plans (e.g. nested loops) that are catastrophic at a billion rows. ANALYZE re-gathers stats — most slow queries in the world come down to stale stats, not bad SQL.

questions.question: What is the selectivity of a predicate?
options: The number of rows in the output after filtering
The number of distinct values in the filtered column
The fraction of input rows that pass the filter, between 0.0 and 1.0
The fraction of pages the query must read from disk
questions.explanation: Selectivity is a fraction (e.g. user_id = 123 → 0.0001, rating IS NOT NULL → 0.95); cardinality is the resulting row count, computed as Output = Input × Selectivity. Confusing the two is the classic slip — one is a ratio, the other a number of rows.

questions.question: A query has two ANDed predicates with selectivities S₁ = 0.1 and S₂ = 0.01. Assuming independence, what selectivity should the planner use, and which access method does the result suggest?
options: 0.11 — medium selectivity, so a bitmap scan
0.001 — very low selectivity (0.1%), so use an index
0.1 — take the larger predicate, so a sequential scan
0.055 — average the two, so a bitmap scan
questions.explanation: AND multiplies: 0.1 × 0.01 = 0.001, well under the ~1% threshold where an index lookup beats scanning. Adding (0.11) is roughly the OR formula's first term (OR is S₁ + S₂ − S₁×S₂); high-selectivity predicates (>10%) are the ones that favor sequential scans.

questions.question: On heavily skewed data, why does a height-balanced histogram give better selectivity estimates than an equi-width one?
options: It stores every distinct value exactly, eliminating estimation error
It uses wavelets to model multi-dimensional distributions
Height-balanced histograms are recomputed on every query, so they never go stale
Equi-width slices the value range evenly, so one bucket swallows nearly all rows; height-balanced gives every bucket 1/B of the rows, so bucket ranges shrink automatically where data is dense
questions.explanation: With equal-width buckets, a hot region lands in one overloaded bucket and any selectivity read off it is wildly wrong. Equal-height buckets adapt their boundaries to density, keeping estimates accurate exactly where skew hurts. Wavelet histograms are a third, separate kind; no histogram stores every value.

questions.question: The stats collector needs an unbiased uniform sample of k rows from an N-row table too big to shuffle, in one streaming pass. Reservoir sampling keeps the first k rows, then swaps row i in with probability k/i. What guarantee does this give?
options: Every row ends up in the sample with equal probability k/N, using O(k) memory and no second pass
The sample always contains the k most frequent values
The sample is biased toward later rows, which are usually fresher
It guarantees each distinct value appears at least once
questions.explanation: Reservoir sampling is exact: the swap probability k/i precisely balances early and late rows so all N have identical inclusion probability. Alternatives trade this exactness for speed — block sampling reads whole pages (biased when rows cluster on disk) and progressive sampling grows until variance is low.

questions.question: Joining Recommendations and Listens on (song_id, user_id), then GROUP BY song_id: why does the sort-merge-join plan get the grouping almost for free, while the hash-partition-join plan pays an extra HP(3) step?
options: SMJ deduplicates the join output, so there are fewer rows to group

SMJ's output is sorted on the join keys and song_id is a prefix of that order, so groups are already contiguous; HPJ's output is partitioned on BOTH keys, so it must be re-partitioned on song_id alone before grouping
HPJ produces its output in random order, so it must be fully sorted before grouping
SMJ runs the GROUP BY inside the merge phase at zero cost
questions.explanation: Order is the asset: rows sorted by (song_id, user_id) have all of each song's rows adjacent, so grouping is a single read-and-write pass. HPJ's partitions split on the composite key don't align with grouping on song_id alone — the same song's rows can sit in different partitions — hence the repartition. It's a repartition (2N-ish), not a full sort, and grouping still costs a read/write pass in both plans.

questions.question: Both candidate plans for the recommendation query end with the same BigSort(4) for ORDER BY count DESC. Why can neither plan skip it?
options: The SQL standard requires a physical sort for every ORDER BY
Only Plan 2 needs it; Plan 1's output is already sorted by count
BigSort also performs the aggregation, so removing it would drop the COUNT
Grouping leaves rows ordered (or partitioned) by song_id, not by the computed count, so a final sort on count is unavoidable
questions.explanation: The count for each song isn't known until grouping finishes, and no earlier operator could have arranged rows by a value that didn't exist yet. So both totals share the final BigSort — the plans differ only in the join term and Plan 2's extra repartition, and the comparison is pure arithmetic: plug in table sizes and pick the smaller number.

questions.question: In PostgreSQL EXPLAIN output, how do you read the plan tree, and what does cost=0.42..1234.56 on an operator mean?
options: Top-down; the two numbers are best-case and worst-case cost
Bottom-up; the numbers are IO cost and CPU cost respectively
Bottom-up (leaves scan first, results bubble to the root); the numbers are startup cost before the first row and total cost for all rows
Top-down; the numbers are estimated and actual runtime in milliseconds
questions.explanation: EXPLAIN is read bottom-up: Seq Scans feed a Hash Join, which feeds HashAggregate, Sort, Limit. cost=startup..total is the optimizer's own unit-cost estimate (not milliseconds, not a best/worst range), and rows= is the estimated row count flowing out of the step.

questions.question: PostgreSQL used HashAggregate for GROUP BY title, artist instead of sorting. When is that a win, and what happens if the assumption breaks?
options: It wins when the input is pre-sorted; otherwise it silently returns unsorted groups
It wins when the number of groups fits in an in-memory hash table (cost ~C_r·P(input), no sort); if not, it spills to disk and falls back to a partition-based (HPJ-style) approach
It always wins, because hashing is asymptotically cheaper than sorting
It wins only when an index exists on the grouped columns
questions.explanation: HashAggregate builds a hash table keyed by group and accumulates counts in one read pass — no BigSort needed — which beats sort-based grouping whenever one-row-per-group output fits in RAM. Our simplified IO model assumes grouping requires sorting, so this is the most common real-optimizer trick to know; the fallback on overflow is partitioning, not failure.

questions.question: You must join a 10 MB dim_artists table with a 1 PB fact table spread over 1,000 nodes. Which shuffle strategy minimizes network cost?
options: Broadcast shuffle — send the tiny table to every node, so the petabyte table never moves
Hash shuffle — redistribute both tables by artist_id so matching keys co-locate
Co-located join — the tables are already partitioned correctly by definition
Round-robin shuffle — spread both tables evenly to balance load
questions.explanation: Broadcast costs small-table-size × #nodes (10 MB × 1,000 = 10 GB), vastly cheaper than hash-shuffling both tables (~total size of both, i.e. a petabyte over the network). Co-located (zero shuffle) is best but only applies when the tables were pre-partitioned on the same key — not a choice you get to make at query time.

questions.question: A GROUP BY over 1,000 nodes uses two-phase reaggregation: each node first groups its own data locally, then partial results are shuffled by the grouping key and merged. What problem does the local pre-aggregation phase solve?
options: It guarantees deterministic ordering of the final results
It prevents any single node from running out of RAM during the join
Without it, billions of tiny raw records would flood the network; pre-aggregating shrinks the data ~1,000× (1M listen rows per node → 1K artist totals) before transfer
It hides node failures, since partial aggregates can be recomputed
questions.explanation: The network is the scarce resource: shipping every raw row to a coordinator would move billions of minuscule records, so each node collapses its slice to per-group partials first, and the global merge over partials preserves exactness. The point is network volume, not ordering or fault tolerance.

questions.question: In Spotify's end-to-end pipeline, the play-button click lands in an LSM store, but the CEO's dashboard reads a columnar warehouse. Why can't one storage format serve both ends?
options: Licensing: OLTP and OLAP engines come from different vendors
LSM stores cannot be replicated, so analytics must copy the data anyway
Columnar files cannot store timestamps, which OLTP requires

The write path needs append-only, no-random-IO ingestion (~8 ms, 100K writes/sec/node), while the scan path needs compressed columns where a query reads 3 of 20 columns over a petabyte — opposite optimizations, bridged by the nightly ETL
questions.explanation: Act 1 optimizes for writes (LSM MemTable append), Act 3 for scans (columnar star schema with broadcast joins), and Act 2 is the 3-hour Spark ETL — hash partition, BigSort, broadcast join, write Parquet — that converts one format into the other. No single structure wins everywhere; each stage uses the one built for its workload.

questions.question: During a live song drop, 50,000 users generate a surge of concurrent play-count updates and a standard B+Tree chokes. Per the capstone's toolbox approach, which structure should absorb the surge?
options: A hash index on song_id for O(1) updates
A clustered B+Tree on (song_id, timestamp)
An LSM tree, keeping partial counts in a MemTable and flushing sequentially to SSTables
H3 geo-hashing to spread the writes across cells
questions.explanation: The bottleneck is random write overhead, and LSM trees convert random writes into sequential flushes — ideal for high-bandwidth telemetry. A hash index still performs a disk write per update, and H3 solves geographic bucketing, not write throughput; the capstone skill is matching each workload to the structure built for it.
